notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Daniel 11:1–22, based on the sources I was able to reach. Each point is followed by its source URL.

---

## Daniel 11:1

**v. 1 — “And I, in the first year of Darius the Mede, stood up to strengthen and protect him.”**

- This verse is widely regarded as belonging with the end of chapter 10, not the start of chapter 11. It is the angel (the supernatural interpreter from ch. 10) speaking, not Daniel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_11_commentary1
- Gill explains that the angel is recounting how he strengthened Darius and Cyrus in their good intentions toward the Jews — specifically in letting Israel go free, return to their land, and rebuild the city and temple. The angel countered demonic opposition in the Persian court. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- Ellicott connects it to the fall of Babylon and the return from Exile: at that time, as at the Exodus, the angel of the Lord went before His people. Also alludes to Daniel 6:22. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- Precept Austin adds that Darius the Mede reaffirmed Cyrus's decree permitting Israel to rebuild the Temple, even decreeing that the full cost be paid from the royal treasury (Ezra 6:8-12). The angel's protection of Darius reflects God's covenant promise to Abraham: “I will bless those who bless you” (Gen. 12:3). https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_11_commentary1

---

## Daniel 11:2

**v. 2 — “Now then, I will tell you the truth: Three more kings will arise in Persia, and then a fourth, who will be far richer than all the others. By the power of his wealth, he will stir up everyone against the kingdom of Greece.”**

- The “three more kings” after Cyrus are generally identified as Cambyses II, Pseudo-Smerdis (or Darius I Hystaspes — sources differ), and a third before Xerxes. The fourth is universally identified as **Xerxes I** (also known as Ahasuerus in Esther), famous for his immense wealth and his massive but failed invasion of Greece in 480 BC. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- Gill notes that some lists omit the impostor Smerdis (who reigned only seven months) as unworthy of mention, consistent with Ptolemy's canon. Gill also details Xerxes' vast army — according to Herodotus, 5,283,220 men plus Carthaginian allies — and how his aggression against Greece provoked the later Greek retaliation under Alexander. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- Ellicott notes that “Greece was in no sense 'a kingdom'” at the time of Xerxes' invasion, which argues against the late-date theory that Daniel was written in the Maccabean period. He also notes that the prophecy may have an eschatological dimension beyond mere history. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- Precept Austin cites the ESV Study Bible: the purpose of these detailed prophecies was to reassure faithful Jews that, though they would be caught between warring empires, God was still in control of history. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_11_commentary1

---

## Daniel 11:3

**v. 3 — “Then a mighty king will arise, who will rule with great authority and do as he pleases.”**

- All consulted sources identify this as **Alexander the Great** (336–323 BC), the “notable horn” of the he-goat in Daniel 8:5-8. He conquered the Persian Empire with astonishing speed and ruled with absolute, self-willed authority. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_11_commentary1
- Gill notes that Alexander “did according to his will” — sacrificing friends at pleasure, conquering whom he wished, and even setting himself up to be worshipped as a deity. His historian Curtius wrote that “he seemed to do with nations whatever he pleased.” https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- Ellicott cautions that while the description fits Alexander, the language is general enough that it could point to a future autocrat in the latter times, of whom Alexander is a type. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- Enduring Word notes the interesting account from Josephus (Antiquities XI.8): when Alexander approached Jerusalem, the high priest Jaddua met him in procession and showed him the Book of Daniel, where Daniel declared that a Greek would destroy Persia. Alexander, recognizing himself, spared Jerusalem and granted it religious toleration. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/

---

## Daniel 11:4

**v. 4 — “But as soon as he is established, his kingdom will be broken up and parceled out toward the four winds of heaven. It will not go to his descendants, nor will it have the authority with which he ruled, because his kingdom will be uprooted and given to others.”**

- Fulfilled in the sudden collapse of Alexander's empire after his death at age 32 (323 BC). Within about 20 years, after the Battle of Ipsus (301 BC), four of his generals divided the empire: **Cassander** (Macedonia and Greece — west), **Lysimachus** (Thrace and Asia Minor — east), **Seleucus I Nicator** (Syria, Babylon, and eastern regions — north), and **Ptolemy I Soter** (Egypt — south). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_11_commentary1
- “Not to his posterity” — Alexander left three possible heirs (a mentally deficient half-brother Philip, a posthumous son Alexander, and an illegitimate son Hercules), but all were eventually murdered in the power struggles among the regents. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- Gill identifies the four winds as Ptolemy (south), Antigonus/Seleucus (north/east), and Cassander (west). He notes that the kingdom was “plucked up” for others besides those — including eventually the Romans. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- Ellicott notes the language is too general to make the identification with Alexander's successors certain — the prophecy may also point to a future self-willed king whose empire is similarly shattered. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- Precept Austin emphasizes that at the time of Daniel, Greece did not even exist as a united empire, making the prophecy remarkable. The subsequent prophecies (vv. 5–35) focus on only two of the four divisions — the Seleucids (North) and Ptolemies (South) — because Israel lay directly between them. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_11_commentary1

---

## Daniel 11:5

**v. 5 — “The king of the South will grow strong, but one of his commanders will grow even stronger and will rule his own kingdom with great authority.”**

- “King of the South” = **Ptolemy I Soter** of Egypt (323–285 BC). He ruled over Egypt, Libya, Cyrene, Ethiopia, Arabia, Phoenicia, Coele-Syria, Cyprus, and parts of Greece. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_11_commentary1
- “One of his commanders” (or princes) = **Seleucus I Nicator**. Seleucus had originally served under Ptolemy after fleeing from Antigonus. With Ptolemy's help (800 infantry and 200 cavalry), Seleucus regained Babylon in 312 BC and eventually built an empire stretching from Asia Minor to India — larger than Ptolemy's. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_11_commentary1 ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- Ellicott notes the Hebrew is obscure: both Greek versions interpret it as “one of the princes of the king of the south shall be stronger than his former master.” It is difficult, Ellicott admits, to see how Seleucus Nicator can be called a “prince” of Ptolemy Soter — yet the traditional identification persists. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html

---

## Daniel 11:6

**v. 6 — “After some years they will form an alliance, and the daughter of the king of the South will go to the king of the North to seal the agreement. But his daughter will not retain her position of power, nor will his strength endure. At that time she will be given up, along with her royal escort and her father and the one who supported her.”**

- “After some years” — about 30 years after the events of v. 5 (~252 BC). The kings are now **Ptolemy II Philadelphus** (South) and **Antiochus II Theos** (North). They had been at war for over a decade and sought peace through a dynastic marriage. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_11_commentary1 ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- “The daughter of the king of the South” = **Berenice** (also spelled Bernice), daughter of Ptolemy II. She was brought to Antiochus II with an enormous dowry of gold and silver. As part of the agreement, Antiochus divorced his existing wife **Laodice** and disinherited her children in favor of Berenice's future offspring. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- “She will not retain her position of power” — When Ptolemy II died, Antiochus II put away Berenice and took Laodice back. Laodice, not trusting her husband, had him poisoned. She then sent assassins to kill Berenice, her infant son, and her Egyptian attendants at Daphne near Antioch. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- Gill notes that “he that strengthened her in these times” may refer to Berenice's brother (Ptolemy III) and supporters from Asia Minor who set out for her relief but arrived too late. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- Ellicott questions whether this marriage really affected the Jewish people in any special way, suggesting the traditional reading is “very unsatisfactory” and that the passage may instead describe a characteristic pattern of political marriages in the end times. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html

---

## Daniel 11:7

**v. 7 — “But one from her family line will rise up in his place, come against the army of the king of the North, and enter his fortress, fighting and prevailing.”**

- “One from her family line” (lit. “a branch of her roots”) = **Ptolemy III Euergetes**, brother of the murdered Berenice. He succeeded their father Ptolemy II on the Egyptian throne and marched into Syria to avenge his sister. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- Ptolemy III invaded the Seleucid kingdom under **Seleucus II Callinicus** (son of Laodice), captured the fortress of Seleucia (the port of Antioch), and prevailed decisively. He took Syria, Cilicia, and territories beyond the Euphrates. Justin says he would have taken the whole Seleucid kingdom had a rebellion in Egypt not called him home. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- Ellicott notes that Theodotion and the LXX translate “army” (δύναμιν), which Theodoret explains as a name for Jerusalem — though Ellicott finds this unlikely. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html

---

## Daniel 11:8

**v. 8 — “He will take even their gods captive to Egypt, with their metal images and their precious vessels of silver and gold. For some years he will stay away from the king of the North.”**

- Ptolemy III carried back to Egypt enormous spoils. Jerome, citing historians, records that Ptolemy took 2,500 captured idols/images into Egypt — many of which were Egyptian gods that Cambyses had earlier carried off to Persia. By restoring these to their temples, Ptolemy earned the title “Euergetes” (Benefactor) from the grateful Egyptians. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- Jerome also reports Ptolemy brought back 40,000 talents of silver and vast quantities of gold and silver vessels. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- “For some years he will stay away from the king of the North” — Ptolemy III outlived Seleucus II by four years (he reigned 25 years total) and there was a period of ceasefire between them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/

---

## Daniel 11:9

**v. 9 — “who will invade the realm of the king of the South and then return to his own land.”**

- The Hebrew is ambiguous about the subject. The traditional reading (reflected in English versions) takes the king of the North (Seleucus II) as the subject: he attempted a counter-invasion of Egypt but achieved nothing and returned home. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- Ellicott notes that according to the Hebrew text, “the king of the south” is in the genitive case (supported by Theodotion and Jerome): “The king of the north shall come into the kingdom of the southern king, and then shall return to his own land — apparently without gaining any advantage.” Justin records that Seleucus fitted out a great fleet which was destroyed by a storm. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- Gill offers an alternative: the verse may simply describe the king of the South coming into the kingdom of the North, ravaging it, and returning home unhindered with great spoil. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm

---

## Daniel 11:10

**v. 10 — “But his sons will stir up strife and assemble a great army, which will advance forcefully, sweeping through like a flood, and will again carry the battle as far as his fortress.”**

- “His sons” = the sons of Seleucus II Callinicus: **Seleucus III Ceraunus** (who ruled only briefly, 226–223 BC) and **Antiochus III the Great** (223–187 BC). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- Antiochus III assembled a massive army, swept down through the Holy Land like a flood, and advanced against the fortress of the king of the South (Ptolemy IV Philopator). He captured Seleucia, Tyre, Ptolemais, and Gaza, and besieged the Egyptians in Sidon. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- Precept Austin notes that from here through v. 19, God prophesies that Syria would gain ascendancy over Egypt and thus gain control of the Holy Land — setting the stage for the persecutions of Antiochus Epiphanes (vv. 21–35). https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_11_commentary1

---

## Daniel 11:11

**v. 11 — “In a rage, the king of the South will march out to fight the king of the North, who will raise a large army, but it will be delivered into the hand of his enemy.”**

- Fulfilled at the **Battle of Raphia** (217 BC). Ptolemy IV Philopator marched out enraged against Antiochus III, who had mustered a great army. Yet the larger Syrian army was routed and handed over to Ptolemy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- Ellicott notes the ambiguity of the Hebrew: some commentators have taken it the opposite way (the northern king defeating the southern), but the clarifying phrase “with the king of the north” and the context of v. 12 confirm that the southern king is the victor here. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html

---

## Daniel 11:12

**v. 12 — “When the army is carried off, the king of the South will be proud in heart and will cast down tens of thousands, but he will not triumph.”**

- After his victory at Raphia, Ptolemy IV's heart was lifted up with pride. He slaughtered tens of thousands of the enemy. Yet he “did not prevail” in the ultimate sense — he failed to follow up his victory decisively. Instead of striking a final blow, he was content merely to regain the towns Antiochus had taken. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- Ellicott notes that the Hebrew could also be read: “the multitude is lifted up — i.e., takes courage — and its heart is exalted,” or “when the multitude takes courage the king's heart is exalted.” The English translation is most in keeping with the context. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- Historically, Ptolemy IV then attempted to enter the Holy Place in Jerusalem (as recorded in 3 Maccabees), but was supernaturally prevented. Ellicott finds it surprising that the prophecy, if written for Jewish comfort, does not allude to this. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html

---

## Daniel 11:13

**v. 13 — “For the king of the North will raise another army, larger than the first, and after some years he will advance with a great army and many supplies.”**

- Antiochus III returned about 13–14 years after Raphia (c. 203–202 BC) with an even larger army and abundant supplies. By this time Ptolemy IV had died and been succeeded by his young son **Ptolemy V Epiphanes** (a mere child), leaving Egypt weakened. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- Ellicott notes “much riches” means all that is necessary for the maintenance of a large army. The invasion of Egypt was coordinated with Philip V of Macedon. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html

---

## Daniel 11:14

**v. 14 — “In those times many will rise up against the king of the South. Violent ones among your own people will exalt themselves in fulfillment of the vision, but they will fail.”**

- “Many will rise up against the king of the South” — during the early years of Ptolemy V Epiphanes, Egypt faced multiple insurrections. Philip of Macedon also allied with Antiochus III against Egypt. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- “Violent ones among your own people” — literally “robbers (or sons of violence) of your people.” This refers to certain Jews who, resenting Ptolemaic rule, joined with Antiochus III against Egypt. They saw themselves as helping fulfill the vision, but “they shall fall” — their revolt failed. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- Ellicott observes that this is the earliest verse where there is any explicit reference to Daniel's people. He notes the significant point is the “falling” of these violent ones — their conduct brought them just the reverse of what they expected. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html

---

## Daniel 11:15

**v. 15 — “Then the king of the North will come, build up a siege ramp, and capture a fortified city. The forces of the South will not stand; even their best troops will not be able to resist.”**

- Fulfilled when Antiochus III captured **Sidon** (c. 198 BC). The Egyptian general Scopas had retaken Jerusalem and parts of Syria while Antiochus was away, but was then besieged by Antiochus at Sidon. The Egyptian forces, even their elite troops, could not withstand the siege and were forced by famine to surrender. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- “Fortified city” — literally “a city of fortifications.” Sidon was heavily fortified; Scopas and his best troops fled there but could not hold out. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html

---

## Daniel 11:16

**v. 16 — “The invader will do as he pleases, and no one will stand against him. He will establish himself in the Beautiful Land, with destruction in his hand.”**

- Antiochus III now held unchallenged authority. He entered the **“Beautiful Land” (the Glorious Land)** — i.e., Palestine / the land of Israel — and did whatever he pleased. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- Enduring Word notes the irony: the Jews had initially welcomed Antiochus III as a liberator from Egyptian rule, but this proved unwise. He came with “destruction in his hand.” https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- Ellicott, however, observes that “history does not speak of any acts of destruction committed by him in Palestine. On the contrary, it is recorded of him that he treated the Jews with kindness.” This discrepancy leads Ellicott to question whether the passage is strictly historical. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html

---

## Daniel 11:17

**v. 17 — “He will resolve to come with the strength of his whole kingdom, and will reach an agreement with the king of the South. He will give him a daughter in marriage in order to overthrow the kingdom, but his plan will not succeed or help him.”**

- Antiochus III, seeking to dominate Egypt, gave his daughter **Cleopatra I** (not the famous Cleopatra VII, but her ancestor) in marriage to the young **Ptolemy V Epiphanes**. He hoped she would be his agent of influence, ultimately delivering Egypt into his hands. The plan backfired: Cleopatra was loyal to her husband, not her father. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- “Daughter of women” (some translations) = simply “a woman.” The phrase “upright ones with him” (KJV) may hint at Jews cooperating with Antiochus's plan, but the Hebrew is obscure. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- The plan “shall not stand” — Antiochus's hope of controlling Egypt through his daughter failed entirely. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/

---

## Daniel 11:18

**v. 18 — “Then he will turn his face to the coastlands and capture many of them. But a commander will put an end to his reproach and will turn it back upon him.”**

- After the Egyptian disappointment, Antiochus III turned his attention to Asia Minor, the Aegean islands, and Greece (“the coastlands”). He took many cities and islands, including Ephesus, aided by the famous Carthaginian general **Hannibal**. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- “A commander” = the Roman general **Lucius Cornelius Scipio** (with his brother Scipio Africanus). At the battles of Thermopylae (191 BC) and Magnesia (190 BC), the Romans decisively defeated Antiochus III. The “reproach” he intended for Greece was turned back on his own head. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- Ellicott notes the Greek versions show considerable variation. He suggests the Hebrew could mean either that a prince causes the reproach to cease (nominative reading) or that the king causes the princes who reproached him to cease (accusative reading). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html

---

## Daniel 11:19

**v. 19 — “After this, he will turn back toward the fortresses of his own land, but he will stumble and fall and be no more.”**

- Humiliated by Rome, Antiochus III retreated to his strongholds in Syria. He had lost all his gains and was burdened with heavy war indemnities to Rome. Desperate for funds, he attempted to pillage a temple of Bel (Baal) in Elymais (Persia) and was killed by enraged local citizens. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- “He shall stumble and fall, and not be found” — his inglorious death ended his reign. He was “no more.” https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/

---

## Daniel 11:20

**v. 20 — “In his place one will arise who will send out a tax collector for the glory of the kingdom; but within a few days he will be destroyed, though not in anger or in battle.”**

- This refers to **Seleucus IV Philopator** (187–175 BC), eldest son of Antiochus III. Burdened by Roman tribute, he sent his tax collector **Heliodorus** through the kingdom — including into “the glorious kingdom” (the Holy Land) — to raise revenue. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- “Within a few days he shall be destroyed, but not in anger or in battle” — Seleucus IV was assassinated (poisoned) after a short reign, likely orchestrated by his brother Antiochus IV Epiphanes. It was not death in war or open conflict but by conspiracy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- Ellicott notes the marginal reading “raiser of taxes” is to be preferred as “exactor” or “oppressor.” The new king causes the “oppressor” to pass through “the majesty of the kingdom.” https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html
- Gill identifies the “raiser of taxes” as Seleucus Philopator and connects him with the attempt to plunder the Jerusalem temple (2 Maccabees 3), which was thwarted by an angelic vision. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- Ellicott marks this verse as a **transition**: the first part of the prophecy (11:2–20) concludes here, and from v. 21 onward the most prominent figure of the prophecy — a person who remains before the reader till the end of the chapter — is introduced. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html

---

## Daniel 11:21

**v. 21 — “In his place a despicable person will arise; royal honors will not be given to him, but he will come in a time of peace and seize the kingdom by intrigue.”**

- Widely and unanimously identified as **Antiochus IV Epiphanes** (175–164 BC), the “little horn” of Daniel 8. He was not the legitimate heir — the throne belonged either to his murdered brother Seleucus IV or to Seleucus's son Demetrius (who was a hostage in Rome). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/ ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm
- “A despicable (vile) person” — his moral character was contemptible. He took the title *Epiphanes* (“Illustrious One” or “God Manifest”), but his enemies called him *Epimanes* (“Madman”). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- “He shall come in peaceably (or 'in a time of peace') and seize the kingdom by intrigue” — apart from murdering his brother, Antiochus IV used flattery, smooth promises, and cunning rather than open force. Adam Clarke notes: “He flattered Eumenes, king of Pergamus, and Attalus his brother, and got their assistance. He flattered the Romans, and sent ambassadors to court their favour. He flattered the Syrians, and gained their concurrence.” https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- Ellicott emphasizes that St. Jerome already noted that while much in this chapter fits Antiochus's career, he functions as a “type” of the Antichrist: “*typum eum volunt Antichristi habere, et quae in illo ex parte praecesserint, in Antichristo ex toto esse complenda*” (“they hold him to be a type of Antichrist, and what was partially fulfilled in him will be fully completed in Antichrist”). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html

---

## Daniel 11:22

**v. 22 — “Then a flood of forces will be swept away before him and destroyed, along with a prince of the covenant.”**

- The two main interpretations of **“prince of the covenant”** are:
  1. **The Jewish high priest Onias III**, who was deposed and later murdered (c. 171 BC) through Antiochus's intrigues. Onias was the legitimate high priest and a defender of the covenant. His brother Jason bribed Antiochus to make him high priest instead, and later Menelaus arranged Onias's assassination. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
  2. **Ptolemy VI Philometor** of Egypt, with whom Antiochus made a treaty (“covenant”) but then acted deceitfully against. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- Enduring Word favors the first reading (Onias III) while also acknowledging the Ptolemy identification. The “flood of forces” swept away refers to the overwhelming armies Antiochus defeated or the overwhelming tide of his own forces. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/
- Ellicott says “this expression is most readily explained” but his text is truncated. He does note that the phrase refers to someone destroyed by the terrible king (the “vile person”), alongside the overwhelming of enemy forces. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html

---

## Summary of Historical Identifications (per the Traditional Reading)

| Verse | Figure/Event | Historical Identity |
|-------|-------------|-------------------|
| 1 | Angel strengthens Darius | Angelic protection of Darius the Mede (538 BC) |
| 2 | Four Persian kings; fourth richest | Cambyses II, Smerdis, Darius I Hystaspes; **Xerxes I** |
| 3 | Mighty king | **Alexander the Great** (336–323 BC) |
| 4 | Kingdom divided to four winds | Four generals: Cassander, Lysimachus, Seleucus, Ptolemy |
| 5 | King of South; his commander | **Ptolemy I Soter**; **Seleucus I Nicator** |

## Where the Traditions Differ

I was unable to reach specific denominational pages from the Lutheran (lcms.org, 1517.org), Reformed (ligonier.org, monergism.com), Methodist (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com), or Catholic/Orthodox (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) sites due to search limits. However, based on the sources I did reach, here is what can be observed about the main differences:

- **Traditional Historicist / Preterist Reading (shared by Gill, Ellicott, Guzik, Precept Austin):** All consulted sources present essentially the same historical identifications — Persian kings → Alexander → Ptolemies and Seleucids → Antiochus IV. This is the mainstream conservative Protestant reading.

- **Ellicott's Cautious Approach (Anglican):** Ellicott repeatedly questions whether the traditional identifications are correct, noting “the difficulties which oppose this interpretation.” He suggests the prophecy may still await its complete fulfilment, with the Ptolemies and Seleucids serving as types of future powers. This is a more cautious, possibly futurist-leaning Anglican reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-11.html

- **Enduring Word / David Guzik (Charismatic / Pentecostal):** Guzik holds the traditional historicist view for vv. 2–35 but, consistent with many Pentecostal and dispensational readings, sees a sharp shift at v. 36 from the historical Antiochus to a future Antichrist. He calls Antiochus “a historical trailer for the ultimate evil man.” https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-11/

- **Gill (older Baptist):** Gill follows the standard historicist scheme through v. 30, but from v. 36 onward identifies “the king” not as a future Antichrist but as the **papal Antichrist** (“the western Antichrist”) — the classic Protestant historicist identification of the Pope. He also sees “the eastern Antichrist” (the Turk/Muslim power) in vv. 40–45. This is a distinctly older Baptist/Reformed historicist view. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/daniel/11.htm

- **Catholic and Orthodox readings:** Not obtained. However, it is well known that Catholic tradition (following Jerome) sees Antiochus IV as the primary referent and a type of Antichrist, but does not identify the Pope with the “king” of vv. 36ff — that is a specifically Protestant historicist reading.

- **Modern scholarship / NET Bible notes:** Not obtained. It is well known that mainstream critical scholarship argues that Daniel 11 is a *vaticinium ex eventu* (prophecy after the fact), written around 164 BC during the Maccabean crisis, and that the break between accurate “prophecy” (history) and failed prediction occurs around v. 40–45.

- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** Spurgeon preached on Daniel 11:32–33 (“the people that know their God shall be strong and do exploits”), applying it to the Maccabean martyrs under Antiochus, but using it as a lesson about the importance of knowledge and understanding for Christian strength and steadfastness. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/knowledge-commended
